text: Terry Alan Kath (January 31, 1946 – January 23, 1978) was an American guitarist and singer best known as a founding member of the rock band Chicago. He played lead guitar and sang lead vocals on many of the band's early hit singles alongside Robert Lamm and Peter Cetera. Praised by his bandmates and other musicians for his guitar skills and his Ray Charles–influenced vocal style, Jimi Hendrix cited Terry Kath as one of his favorite guitarists and considered him "the best guitarist in the universe." Born to Raymond Elmer "Ray" Kath (1912–2003) and Evelyn Meline (nee Haugen) Kath (1916–1982) on January 31, 1946, in Chicago, he grew up in the Norwood Park neighborhood and attended Taft High School. He had an older brother, Rod Kath, and his brother played the drums while his mother played the banjo; Kath also attempted to learn these instruments. He acquired a guitar and amplifier in ninth grade, with early influences including The Ventures, Johnny Smith, Dick Dale, and Howard Roberts, later expanding to George Benson, Kenny Burrell, Mike Bloomfield, Eric Clapton, and Jimi Hendrix. Unlike other Chicago members, Kath was mostly self-taught and enjoyed jamming; in a 1971 interview, he stated he had tried professional lessons but abandoned them, saying "All I wanted to do was play those rock and roll chords." He joined his first semi-professional band, The Mystics, in 1963, then moved to Jimmy Rice and the Gentlemen in 1965, and later played bass in Jimmy Ford and the Executives, where he served as bandleader. He became close friends with Walter Parazaider and Danny Seraphine, who later joined his band. In 1966, Kath joined the Missing Links, taking Parazaider and Seraphine with him, and began playing clubs and ballrooms in Chicago. James William Guercio, who later became Chicago's producer, was a lead guitarist in one of the road bands performing with the Missing Links. Kath declined an offer to play bass for the Illinois Speed Press and move to Los Angeles, choosing instead to focus on guitar and singing. He stayed with Parazaider, Seraphine, and Lee Loughnane, who recruited trombonist James Pankow and vocalist/keyboardist Robert Lamm. The group practiced at Parazaider's parents' basement and changed its name to The Big Thing. After adding Peter Cetera, they moved to Los Angeles and signed with Columbia Records, renaming themselves Chicago Transit Authority, which was shortened to Chicago in mid-1969 due to a legal objection from the real Chicago Transit Authority. Kath was regarded as the band's bandleader and best soloist, with his vocal and jazz and hard rock influences integral to their early sound. He has been praised for his guitar skills and described by rock author Corbin Reiff as "one of the most criminally underrated guitarists to have ever set finger to fretboard." According to Lee Loughnane, Kath could sing lead vocals and play lead and rhythm guitar simultaneously. The group's first album, Chicago Transit Authority (1969), includes Kath's composition "Introduction," described as "Terry's masterpiece" by Dawayne Bailey, which blends jazz, blues, salsa, rock and roll, acid rock, and pop. The album also features "Free Form Guitar," a nearly seven-minute instrumental recorded live in one take using a Fender Dual Showman amplifier pre-amped with a Bogen Challenger P.A. amp, with the guitar's neck held together by a radiator hose clamp. "Beginnings" includes acoustic rhythm guitar by Kath. On the second album, Kath contributed an extended guitar solo to "25 or 6 to 4," a live favorite, and collaborated with Peter Matz on the four-part suite "Memories of Love," singing the lead vocal. Kath wrote at least one song and contributed at least one lead vocal to every Chicago album released during his lifetime. While 1976's Chicago X is best known for Cetera's number one hit "If You Leave Me Now," Kath's "Once or Twice" demonstrated his continued songwriting. He contributed the funky "Mississippi Delta City Blues" and the aggressive "Takin' It on Uptown" on Chicago XI. After his death, the band considered disbanding but was persuaded by Doc Severinsen to continue. Donnie Dacus replaced him, and the band composed and published "Alive Again" on their first album without him, Hot Streets, and later released "Feel the Spirit" in his honor. Kath used several guitars, including a Register guitar costing $80 during The Big Thing era, a Fender Stratocaster, a Gibson SG Standard, a Gibson SG Custom, and a 1969 Les Paul "Professional" model with unconventional low-impedance pickups and a special impedance-matching transformer. He favored light strings, using a tenor guitar string for the top E and moving all regular strings down. For acoustic parts, he played an Ovation acoustic guitar. In the latter part of his career, he favored a heavily modified Fender Telecaster, with the black pickguard and neck-position pickup removed, the hole enlarged and fitted with a Gibson humbucker, the control plate reversed, and decorated with 25 Pignose stickers, a Maico motorcycles decal, and a Chicago Blackhawks logo. He was an early investor in Pignose and served in its management. Most of his guitars had gone missing, including the famous "Pignose" Telecaster; they were later found by his daughter Michelle Kath Sinclair at her step-grandmother's home, including the "Pignose" Telecaster, an Ovation acoustic, a Fender Stratocaster, and a Gibson SG Custom with pickups removed. Kath experimented with various amplification and distortion devices and frequently used a wah-wah pedal. He was interested in playing without a pick and attempted to build an auto-picking device using a modified electrical cocktail mixer. Kath sang lead vocals on several early Chicago songs, including "I'm a Man," "Colour My World," "Make Me Smile," "Movin' In," "In The Country," "Free," "Dialogue (Part I & II)," "Wishing You Were Here," and "Brand New Love Affair." His vocal delivery was described by Robert Lamm as "The White Ray Charles," and Pankow said rehearsing the song with others, he settled on Kath, calling it "bingo – 'that' was the voice." He was one of three primary lead singers, with a vocal range between Cetera's higher tenor and Lamm's fuller, lower baritone, often collaborating with Cetera on songs like "Dialogue (Part I & II)," "Ain't It Blue," "In The Country," and "Brand New Love Affair." He also played lead guitar and sang lead vocals on the closing song "Tell Me" in the 1973 film Electra Glide in Blue, which was used in the final episode of Miami Vice. Kath struggled with health issues and substance abuse, including alcohol. Seraphine recalled that Kath had a high tolerance for drugs and told him, "I'm going to get things under control... if I don't, this stuff is going to kill me," and that he was becoming increasingly unhappy. The night before his death, he visited bandmate Laudir de Oliveira, who offered him tea and they spent the night talking. Guercio said Kath was finishing a solo album before his death, and Pankow denied that Kath was suicidal. Kath enjoyed target shooting and by 1978 was regularly carrying guns. On January 23, 1978, after a party at Don Johnson's home in Woodland Hills, Los Angeles, he began playing with his guns, spinning an unloaded .38 revolver, placing it to his temple and pulling the trigger. Johnson warned him multiple times, and when Kath picked up a semi-automatic 9 mm pistol, he said, "Don't worry about it... Look, the clip is not even in it," and his last words were, "What do you think I'm gonna do? Blow my brains out?" To calm Johnson, Kath showed him the empty magazine, then replaced it, put the gun to his temple, and pulled the trigger. Unbeknownst to him, the gun had a round in the chamber, and he died instantly, eight days shy of his 32nd birthday. He left behind his wife, Camelia Ortiz, and a 20-month-old daughter, Michelle Kath (now Michelle Kath Sinclair). Kath is interred near his parents, Raymond and Evelyn Kath, in the Forest Lawn Memorial Park Cemetery in Glendale, California, in the Gardens of Remembrance. The band was devastated by his death and considered disbanding but continued under Doc Severinsen's persuasion. Kath's position was filled by Donnie Dacus, and at concerts, Lee Loughnane and Robert Lamm have performed lead vocals originally sung by Kath. Some band members have claimed Kath's contributions were overlooked, with Walter Parazaider stating, "If [Kath] was totally up front, he would have gotten a lot more recognition," and noting that Jimi Hendrix once said to him after a show at the Whisky a Go Go, "your guitar player is better than me." In September 1997, Chicago released Chicago Presents The Innovative Guitar of Terry Kath, a CD remembrance on their own Chicago Records label. In 2010, Parazaider said he was unsure whether Kath would have stayed with Chicago or started a solo career, describing him as a free spirit and stating it was 50/50. In 2012, Michelle Kath Sinclair announced funding for a documentary titled Searching for Terry: Discovering a Guitar Legend, which was planned for release in 2016 after interviews with all band members except Cetera. The film premiered at the 2016 Toronto International Film Festival under the name The Terry Kath Experience, with Peter Cetera listed among the cast, and made its U.S. premiere at DOC NYC in November 2016. It was acquired by FilmRise for a 2017 release, premiered on AXS TV in November 2017 as Chicago: The Terry Kath Experience, and was released as VOD and DVD on December 12. The film includes interviews with guitarists Jeff Lynne, Steve Lukather, Mike Campbell, Dean DeLeo, and Joe Walsh, who praised Kath's work, with Walsh calling him "a great guy; a brilliant musician; a songwriter and a great singer; such a monster on guitar; a total experimenter." On April 8, 2016, Chicago was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, with Michelle Kath Sinclair accepting the award on her father's behalf.
